title: JC H2 physics — mechanics: circular motion and gravitation

scenes.caption: Circular motion needs a centre-seeking push
scenes.narration: A satellite stays on its circular path only because something keeps pulling it towards the centre. The blue arrow is that pull: it always points at the centre, no matter where the satellite is on its orbit.

shape.explain: The orbit path: the satellite must follow this circle.
The planet: its gravity is the centre-seeking force.
The satellite in circular motion.
The centripetal force arrow: centre-seeking.
The rule: the force always points to the centre.

steps.text: The centre-seeking pull follows the satellite around

scenes.caption: How big is the centre-seeking force
scenes.narration: The centre-seeking acceleration is v squared over r: spin twice as fast and it quadruples; double the radius and it halves. Multiply by the mass and you have the centripetal force, m v squared over r.

shape.explain: Centripetal acceleration: a = v squared over r.
Centripetal force: F = m v squared over r.

The multiplier: double the velocity.
The radius control chip.
Labels the chip as radius r.
The multiplier: double the radius.
The readout: F goes 1 -> 4 when v doubles, 4 -> 2 when r doubles.

steps.text: Faster spin quadruples the pull; wider turn halves it

scenes.caption: Gravity holds the Moon in orbit
scenes.narration: For the Moon, gravity itself supplies the centripetal force: F equals G M m over r squared. The same pull that weighs you on a bathroom scale keeps the Moon circling the Earth — every orbit is a continuous fall towards the centre.

shape.explain: The Earth: its gravity pulls the Moon.
The Moon in orbit.
The gravitational force arrow: the Moon pulled toward Earth.
Newton's law of gravitation: F = G M m / r squared.

shape.text: G is tiny: 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²
shape.explain: A reminder: G is tiny, 6.67 x 10^-11 N m^2 kg^-2.

steps.text: Every orbit is a fall that keeps missing Earth

scenes.caption: Geostationary orbits hover over one spot
scenes.narration: A geostationary satellite orbits above the equator with a period of exactly 24 hours, turning at the same rate as the Earth below. From the ground it seems to hang motionless in the sky — perfect for weather and broadcast satellites.

shape.explain: The satellite's home point: it stays over one spot.
The radius line to geostationary height.
The geostationary period: T = 24 hours.

A non-geostationary satellite: it drifts away from its spot.

scenes.caption: Misconception: the fling-off force
scenes.narration: A common mistake: thinking a centrifugal force flings you outward in a sharp turn. No outward fling exists: your body wants to keep going straight while the seat pushes you inward - the inward push is the real force.
